content: Starch, with the chemical formula (C6H10O5)n and CAS number 9005-25-8, is a polysaccharide composed of two glucose polymers: amylose and amylopectin. These polymers are typically present in a ratio of 20:80 or 30:70. Both amylose and amylopectin are complex carbohydrates derived from glucose (C6H12O6), making starch a glucose polymer as well. In human nutrition, starch is the most widely consumed polysaccharide and serves as a major source of dietary carbohydrates. It accounts for more than half of the carbohydrate intake in affluent diets and an even greater proportion in less affluent diets. Staple foods such as cereals, roots, and tubers are the primary sources of dietary starch. Starch, particularly cornstarch, is commonly used in cooking to thicken foods like sauces. In industrial applications, starch is utilized in the production of adhesives, paper, textiles, and as a mold in the manufacturing of sweets like jelly beans and wine gums. Starch is typically a white, tasteless, and odorless powder, depending on its source. It is found in the fruits, seeds, rhizomes, or tubers of plants and provides energy when consumed. Major global sources of starch include rice, wheat, corn, and potatoes. Cooked starch-containing foods include boiled rice, bread, noodles, and pasta. Arrowroot and tapioca are also used as food additives for processing. Other commonly used starch sources include arracacha, buckwheat, banana, barley, cassava, kudzu, oca, sago, sorghum, sweet potato, taro, and yams. Edible beans such as fava beans, lentils, and peas are also rich in starch. Pre-cooked starches, known as pregelatinized starches, can thicken cold foods, while uncooked starches require heat to gelatinize. The gelatinization temperature varies depending on the type of starch. Modified food starches undergo chemical modifications to withstand high heat and shear during food processing. Food starches are widely used as thickeners and stabilizers in products like puddings, custards, soups, sauces, gravies, pie fillings, and salad dressings. Resistant starch, which escapes digestion in the small intestine, is another form of starch. Plants store excess glucose as starch, which they later use as an energy source during mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation. In non-food applications, papermaking is the largest global consumer of starch, using millions of metric tons annually. In a typical sheet of copy paper, starch content can reach up to 8%. Both chemically modified and unmodified starches are used in papermaking. In the wet-end process, cationic starches (starches with a positive charge) are used to bind with anionic (negatively charged) paper fibers and fillers, providing wet and dry strength to the paper. In the dry-end process, starch paste solutions, which have been chemically or enzymatically depolymerized, are applied to the paper web to enhance strength and improve water resistance for better printing properties. Corrugating glues, the second-largest non-food starch application, are used in the production of corrugated fiberboard (cardboard). These glues contain a mixture of modified and unmodified starches that are partially gelatinized to form an opaque paste. This paste is applied to the flute tips of the interior fluted paper to bond it to the outer paper layers, providing strength and rigidity to the cardboard boxes after drying under high heat. In the construction industry, starch is used in the manufacturing of wallboard. Starches act as adhesives for the cured gypsum rock and paper covering, adding rigidity to the board. Laundry starch, a liquid prepared by mixing vegetable starch with water, was historically used to stiffen clothing during laundering. In the 16th and 17th centuries, starch was widely used in Europe to stiffen wide collars and ruffs made of fine linen. In the 19th and early 20th centuries, starch was applied to men's shirt collars and sleeves and girls' petticoat ruffles to create smooth, crisp edges. Starch also served a practical purpose by trapping dirt and sweat, which could be easily washed away along with the starch. After each laundering, starch was reapplied. Starch is also used in the production of packing peanuts and some dropped ceiling tiles. In the printing industry, food-grade starch is used to manufacture anti-set-off spray powder, which prevents wet ink from transferring between printed sheets. Starch is also used in the production of bookbinding glues. Additionally, starch can be utilized to produce hydrogen. In the production of gummed sweets like jelly beans and wine gums, starch is used as a mold. A tray is filled with starch and leveled, and a positive mold is pressed into the starch to create impressions. The mixture is then poured into these impressions and set in a stove, reducing the need for conventional molds. Starch solutions are used to test for iodine. A blue-black color indicates the presence of iodine, as iodine molecules fit into the coils of amylose. A standard starch indicator solution is prepared by dissolving 4 grams of soluble starch in 1 liter of heated water, which is then cooled before use. The starch-iodine complex becomes unstable at temperatures above 35°C. This complex is often used in redox titrations, where the solution turns blue in the presence of an oxidizing agent and loses its color in the presence of a reducing agent due to the breakdown of triiodide ions into iodide ions. Starch can be hydrolyzed into simpler carbohydrates using acids, enzymes, or a combination of both. The degree of conversion is measured by the dextrose equivalent (DE), which represents the fraction of glycosidic bonds broken in the starch. Products derived from starch hydrolysis include maltodextrin (a lightly hydrolyzed starch with DE 10–20, used as a filler and thickener), various corn syrups (DE 30–70, used as sweeteners and thickeners in processed foods), dextrose (DE 100, commercial glucose produced by complete hydrolysis of starch), and high-fructose syrup (produced by treating dextrose solutions with glucose isomerase to convert glucose into fructose). In the United States, high-fructose corn syrup is the primary sweetener in sweetened beverages due to its higher sweetness compared to glucose, allowing for reduced sweetener usage.
